hints: Trace the air pathway down from the trachea - what is the name of the first pair of tubes that split off, one to each lung?
walkthrough:
Follow the airway branching**
Think of the trachea as a single windpipe in the neck. At the base it divides into two, one tube going to the right lung and one to the left lung. That first division is a specific named pair of airways.

hints: Start by deciding which circulation each artery belongs to - one branches from the aorta to supply a tissue, the other goes to the lungs for gas exchange.
Now think about what that means for the blood inside - oxygen and carbon dioxide content, pressure, and which side of the heart it came from.
walkthrough:
Separate supply from exchange**
The lower trachea is just a tissue that needs respiring, like any other body tissue. So its arteries branch from the aorta. That is systemic circulation, coming from the left side of the heart.

Contrast with the pulmonary artery**
Arteries to the alveoli are different - they bring deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs to pick up oxygen. So compared to tracheal arteries they carry blood with more carbon dioxide and less oxygen, at lower pressure, and are not part of the systemic aorta supply.

Final answer: Arteries to lower trachea carry oxygenated blood with lower carbon dioxide concentration at higher pressure as part of systemic circulation from the aorta / left side of heart. Arteries to alveoli carry deoxygenated blood as part of pulmonary circulation.

hints: Look at layer T lining the lumen on the left - what two cell types make up the tracheal lining for mucus production and movement?
Zoom in on cell shape and surface - are the cells tall or flat, and what hair-like projections face the air space?
Look at nuclear arrangement and extra detail - where are nuclei positioned and what pale-staining cells are scattered among the epithelium?
walkthrough:
Recognise the lining tissue**
T is the layer right next to the white air space (lumen). In the trachea this is ciliated epithelium containing mucus-secreting goblet cells. That combination traps dust and moves mucus up.

Describe what you can see**
The epithelial cells are tall and columnar. On their free apical edge facing the lumen you can see fine cilia. Between them are paler goblet cells.

Add fine structural detail**
Nuclei are at different heights giving a pseudostratified look, with goblet cell nuclei pushed to the base. The tissue sits on a basement membrane. All of these are visible at x360 in Fig. 1.1.

Final answer: Tissue T is ciliated epithelium with goblet cells. Columnar cells with cilia on apical surface facing lumen. Goblet cells scattered between, with basal nuclei; pseudostratified appearance with basement membrane.

hints: Look at the small round white spaces labelled X near the mucous gland - what type of tiny transport tube has a hollow lumen in connective tissue?
Check what is inside the lumen and how thick the wall is - what cells and contents point to blood rather than air or gland?
Focus on the wall cells themselves - what very thin, flat cells with bulging nuclei form the wall of the smallest blood vessels?
walkthrough:
Name structure X**
X is a small circular profile with a clear central lumen sitting in the connective tissue below the epithelium. That size and position fits a small blood vessel, a capillary or venule supplying the tracheal wall.

Use the lumen contents**
Inside the lumen you can see red blood cells. That immediately tells you it carries blood, not air or mucus. Glands have secretions, vessels have blood cells.

Use the wall structure**
The wall is extremely thin, only one cell thick. It is made of flat endothelial cells with prominent or bulging nuclei. The overall size is very small with a narrow lumen, exactly as expected for a capillary.

Final answer: Structure X is a blood vessel / capillary / venule. Lumen contains red blood cells. Wall is very thin endothelium one cell thick of flat cells with prominent bulging nuclei; small narrow lumen.
